**Cosine annealing gradually reduces the step size within a cycle.** It starts near a chosen maximum, moves smoothly toward a minimum, and slows refinement near the end. A warm restart raises the learning rate again while retaining learned weights. [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html)

At the start of a cycle, the cosine term is one and the schedule returns the maximum. Halfway through, it returns the midpoint of maximum and minimum. At the end, it reaches the minimum. Longer later cycles can give progressively more time for refinement.

**Restarting the rate is not restarting the model.** The network does not return to random weights. Optimizer-state treatment depends on the chosen implementation and should be documented. The higher-rate phase can explore beyond the current local region, but it can also disturb a good solution.

Compare against a simpler decay schedule at equal optimizer updates. Express the cycle lengths in the units actually advanced by the scheduler, especially with gradient accumulation. Select checkpoints using independent validation rather than assuming the last cycle endpoint is always best.

**Technical details and references.**

Cosine annealing smoothly lowers learning rate within a cycle; warm restarts reset it to a larger value to explore a new region while retaining model weights. A common schedule is [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html)

$$\eta_t=\eta_{min}+\tfrac12(\eta_{max}-\eta_{min})(1+\cos(\pi T_{cur}/T_i)).$$

Cycle lengths may grow over training. A restart is not reinitializing the network, and optimizer-state handling must match the chosen implementation. Benefits depend on task and budget; compare with simpler decay under equal updates. Save validation-selected checkpoints and report the schedule in optimizer steps, especially when changing batch size or accumulation.
